title: Explain Flink's architecture — the Dispatcher (job submission + REST/dashboard), JobManager (master: schedules tasks, converts the JobGraph into a physical execution plan, coordinates checkpoints/recovery), ResourceManager (allocates TaskManager slots via YARN/K8s/standalone), and TaskManagers (workers whose "slots" are the execution units) — and walk the flow of a submitted job through them.

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Flink's runtime is a master-worker architecture made of four components. The Dispatcher receives submitted jobs over REST, serves the web dashboard, and spawns a JobManager per job. The JobManager is the master that converts the logical JobGraph into a physical ExecutionGraph, schedules tasks, requests resources, and coordinates checkpoints and recovery. The ResourceManager allocates execution slots on TaskManagers from the underlying cluster manager, whether standalone, YARN, or Kubernetes. The TaskManagers are the worker processes whose slots actually run the task threads and exchange data.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India runs a large back-office processing operation. The Dispatcher is the front desk that receives new work orders and the public status board everyone checks. For each work order it appoints a project manager, the JobManager, who takes the high-level plan, turns it into a detailed step-by-step execution plan, assigns the steps to staff, and keeps the master checkpoint so that if anything crashes the work resumes from the last safe point. The ResourceManager is the staffing coordinator who finds free desks for the workers, drawing from whatever office building the bank is using. The TaskManagers are the actual clerks sitting at desks, and each desk, a slot, is one unit of work capacity where the real processing happens and where clerks pass documents to each other.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Flink's runtime is a master-worker architecture made of four components. The Dispatcher receives submitted jobs over REST, serves the web dashboard, and spawns a JobManager per job. The JobManager is the master that converts the logical JobGraph into a physical ExecutionGraph, schedules tasks, requests resources, and coordinates checkpoints and recovery. The ResourceManager allocates execution slots on TaskManagers from the underlying cluster manager, whether standalone, YARN, or Kubernetes. The TaskManagers are the worker processes whose slots actually run the task threads and exchange data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India runs a large back-office processing operation. The Dispatcher is the front desk that receives new work orders and the public status board everyone checks. For each work order it appoints a project manager, the JobManager, who takes the high-level plan, turns it into a detailed step-by-step execution plan, assigns the steps to staff, and keeps the master checkpoint so that if anything crashes the work resumes from the last safe point. The ResourceManager is the staffing coordinator who finds free desks for the workers, drawing from whatever office building the bank is using. The TaskManagers are the actual clerks sitting at desks, and each desk, a slot, is one unit of work capacity where the real processing happens and where clerks pass documents to each other.

**One line to remember:** Flink's runtime is Dispatcher receives jobs and serves the UI, JobManager plans and schedules and checkpoints each job, ResourceManager allocates slots from the cluster manager, and TaskManagers run the work in their slots.

sections.s2_technical:
Flink separates the control plane that coordinates a job from the data plane that executes it. When you write a Flink program, the API builds a logical dataflow called the JobGraph, a directed graph of operators like sources, transformations, and sinks. You submit this to the cluster, and the four runtime components take over.

The Dispatcher is the entry point of a Flink cluster. It exposes the REST endpoint that the command-line client and other tools use to submit jobs, and it serves the web dashboard where you watch running jobs, metrics, and checkpoints. For each submitted job the Dispatcher starts a dedicated JobManager, so the Dispatcher is long-lived while JobManagers are per-job. The JobManager, sometimes called the master, is the brain of a single job. It receives the JobGraph and transforms it into the ExecutionGraph, the physical plan that accounts for parallelism, so a source operator with parallelism four becomes four parallel subtasks. The JobManager then schedules these subtasks onto available slots, tracks their status, triggers periodic checkpoints that snapshot the state of all operators to durable storage, and on a failure it coordinates recovery by restoring from the last completed checkpoint and rescheduling the affected tasks. Internally the JobManager contains the scheduler and the checkpoint coordinator.

The ResourceManager is responsible for acquiring and managing TaskManager slots. It is pluggable to different deployment backends: in standalone mode the TaskManagers are already running and register their slots, while under YARN or Kubernetes the ResourceManager dynamically requests new TaskManager containers from the cluster manager when a job needs more slots and releases them when idle. A slot is the unit of resource isolation on a TaskManager, representing a fixed slice of its memory, and the number of slots per TaskManager is configured. The TaskManagers are the worker processes, also called workers. Each runs one or more task slots, and each slot executes the subtasks assigned to it as threads, holds the operator state, and manages the network buffers through which subtasks exchange data streams, both within a TaskManager and across the network to other TaskManagers.

Walking a job through the system: you submit the packaged job to the Dispatcher over REST. The Dispatcher starts a JobManager for it. The JobManager builds the ExecutionGraph from the JobGraph, computing the parallel subtasks, and asks the ResourceManager for the required number of slots. The ResourceManager allocates slots on existing TaskManagers or, under YARN or Kubernetes, spins up new TaskManager containers to provide them, and the TaskManagers register their offered slots. The JobManager deploys each subtask into a slot, the TaskManagers run them and stream data between them according to the plan, and the JobManager periodically triggers checkpoints that each TaskManager participates in by snapshotting its state. If a TaskManager fails, the JobManager detects it, restores the whole job from the last checkpoint, and reschedules. When the job finishes, slots are freed and, in dynamic deployments, idle TaskManagers are released. A senior-level nuance is the high-availability setup, where the JobManager's metadata is stored in a highly available service like ZooKeeper or Kubernetes so a standby JobManager can take over if the leader fails, which matters for long-running streaming jobs. Another nuance is slot sharing, where subtasks of different operators in the same job can share a slot to use resources efficiently, which affects how many slots a job actually needs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a real-time fraud-scoring streaming job must run continuously over the transaction stream, and the team needs to understand how Flink will deploy and run it so they can size the cluster and reason about recovery. They do not grasp which component does what, so when a worker crashed they did not know what recovered the job. This is exactly why understanding the architecture matters: the Dispatcher accepts the job, the JobManager plans and checkpoints it, the ResourceManager finds slots, and the TaskManagers run it, and on failure the JobManager restores from the last checkpoint.

This is exactly how Flink's architecture works. Each component has a clear role, and tracing a job through submission, planning, slot allocation, execution, checkpointing, and recovery explains the whole lifecycle.

Problem 2 — The team wanted to confirm that a TaskManager crash would not lose state and would resume from a checkpoint rather than restart from zero. That recovery is coordinated by the JobManager using the last completed checkpoint, re-requesting slots if needed. This is the checkpoint-and-recovery responsibility.

Because running a real Flink cluster is heavy, this runnable demo models the four components and the job lifecycle. A `Dispatcher` accepts a submitted `JobGraph` and starts a `JobManager`. The `JobManager` builds an execution plan, requests slots from a `ResourceManager`, deploys subtasks to `TaskManager` slots, triggers checkpoints, and on a simulated TaskManager failure restores from the last checkpoint. The demo submits a fraud-scoring job, shows planning, slot allocation, execution, a checkpoint, a worker crash, and recovery from the checkpoint.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# flink-conf.yaml
jobmanager.rpc.address: jobmanager
taskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots: 4
parallelism.default: 4
execution.checkpointing.interval: 10s
high-availability: zookeeper
state.backend: rocksdb
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cluster with a ResourceManager and two TaskManagers of four slots each, and a fraud-scoring job with four operators at parallelism two.

Step 1: The job is submitted to the Dispatcher over REST. The Dispatcher logs that it received the job, shows it on the dashboard, and spawns a dedicated JobManager for this one job.

Step 2: The JobManager builds the ExecutionGraph from the JobGraph, expanding the four operators at parallelism two into eight parallel subtasks, which is the physical plan that accounts for parallelism.

Step 3: The JobManager asks the ResourceManager for enough slots for the eight subtasks. The ResourceManager checks the registered TaskManagers, notes it has enough live slots, and in a YARN or Kubernetes deployment it would spin up new TaskManagers if there were not enough.

Step 4: The JobManager deploys each subtask into a TaskManager slot, and the TaskManagers log running each subtask, which is where the actual stream processing happens, with data flowing between subtasks through network buffers.

Step 5: The JobManager triggers checkpoints. Each live TaskManager snapshots its operator state to durable storage, and the JobManager marks the checkpoint complete. A periodic checkpoint runs again while the job is running, advancing the checkpoint id.

Step 6: One TaskManager crashes, losing its slots and the subtasks it was running. The JobManager detects the failure and recovers by restoring from the last completed checkpoint, re-requesting slots, and redeploying the affected subtasks, so no state is lost and the job resumes from the checkpoint rather than from zero.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink's runtime is a master-worker architecture with four components, and I like to describe each by its job. The Dispatcher is the entry point: it receives submitted jobs over REST, serves the web dashboard, and spawns a dedicated JobManager for each job, so the Dispatcher is long-lived while JobManagers are per-job. The JobManager is the master of a single job and the brain of the operation: it converts the logical JobGraph into the physical ExecutionGraph, expanding operators according to their parallelism into parallel subtasks, schedules those subtasks onto slots, and crucially runs the checkpoint coordinator that periodically snapshots all operator state to durable storage and, on a failure, restores the job from the last completed checkpoint. The ResourceManager acquires and manages execution slots and is pluggable to the deployment backend, so in standalone mode it uses already-running TaskManagers while under YARN or Kubernetes it dynamically requests new TaskManager containers when more slots are needed and releases them when idle. The TaskManagers are the worker processes, and each has a fixed number of slots that actually run the subtask threads, hold the operator state, and exchange data streams through network buffers.

Walking a job through the system: you submit the packaged job to the Dispatcher, which starts a JobManager. The JobManager builds the ExecutionGraph and asks the ResourceManager for the required slots. The ResourceManager allocates them on existing TaskManagers or spins up new ones under YARN or Kubernetes, and the TaskManagers register their slots. The JobManager deploys each subtask into a slot, the TaskManagers run them and stream data between them, and the JobManager triggers checkpoints that each TaskManager participates in by snapshotting its state. If a TaskManager fails, the JobManager detects it, restores the job from the last checkpoint, re-requests slots, and reschedules, so no state is lost. The high-availability setup stores the JobManager metadata in a service like ZooKeeper or Kubernetes so a standby can take over if the leader dies, which matters for long-running streaming jobs, and slot sharing lets subtasks of different operators share a slot to use resources efficiently.

At the National Bank of India we ran a continuous real-time fraud-scoring job on Flink, and understanding this architecture was exactly what let us size the cluster and reason about recovery. When a TaskManager crashed in production, we knew it was the JobManager that detected the failure and restored the job from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from zero, which is why our fraud state survived the crash. Being able to trace a job from the Dispatcher accepting it, to the JobManager planning and checkpointing it, to the ResourceManager finding slots, to the TaskManagers executing it, is what let the team operate the job confidently and tune its parallelism and checkpoint interval sensibly.
